stories.title: New York City’s First El Pollo Loco Coming to Jackson Heights in Queens
stories.excerpt: Why did the chicken cross the continent? To get to new customers on the other side. Popular fast-casual grilled chicken restaurant El Pollo Loco has signed a lease to open its first-ever East Coast location in New York City, Commercial Observer has learned. El Pollo Loco signed a 10-year lease for 2,400 square feet at 37-07 82nd Street in Jackson Heights, Queens, according to tenant broker Ripco Real Estate. It is expected to open in 2027. The asking rent was not disclosed, but the average asking rent for retail space in Jackson Heights ranges between $45 and $65 per square foot, according to data from RI Manhattan Realty. Dillon Ross and Jon Paul Pirraglia from Ripco represented the tenant in this deal. “Bringing El Pollo Loco to New York City marks a defining moment for the brand as it expands into one of the country’s most dynamic retail and restaurant markets,” Ross said in a statement. “Jackson Heights offers the exceptional foot traffic, diverse customer base and neighborhood energy that make it an ideal location for El Pollo Loco’s first East Coast restaurant.” Anthony Pastecchi from Kent Realty represented the landlord, Hampton Associates, in the deal. El Pollo Loco’s new spot will be in the ground-floor retail space along 82nd Street, which was previously occupied by Burger King. “We’re excited to welcome El Pollo Loco to Jackson Heights for its first East Coast location,” Pastecchi said in a statement. “The neighborhood’s strong pedestrian traffic, diverse community and thriving retail environment make it an ideal fit for the brand’s New York City debut.” The chain restaurant, which did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment, is best known for its Mexican-style grilled chicken. El Pollo Loco has nearly 500 locations across the West Coast, including in California, Arizona, Colorado, Louisiana, Nevada, Texas and Utah. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: El Pollo Loco signs first East Coast location: 2,400 SF, Jackson Heights Queens, 2027 opening
10-year lease at $45–$65/SF asking rent reflects strong neighborhood retail demand
Demonstrates QOZ/emerging neighborhood retail anchoring, signals population density & foot traffic growth
stories.summary: El Pollo Loco, a West Coast fast-casual chain, has leased 2,400 SF in Jackson Heights, Queens for its first East Coast store, opening in 2027 at market rents of $45–$65/SF. The deal underscores Jackson Heights' appeal as a high-foot-traffic, diverse neighborhood anchoring retail tenancy. The chain's cross-country expansion signals investor confidence in Queens' demographic and economic trajectory.
stories.impact: Jackson Heights/Queens retail maturation reflects underlying multifamily demand strength in outer boroughs. Anchor retail leasing (especially national brand expansion) typically precedes or accelerates multifamily inflow; strong foot traffic and mixed-use vibrancy drive renter preference and rent growth. Developer should monitor Jackson Heights/Long Island City corridor for acquisition or development windows ahead of retail-driven neighborhood inflection.

stories.title: Walmart Development Set for Palm Beach County
stories.excerpt: Walmart has paid $11.7 million for development land by the western end of Palm Beach County, Fla., in the latest example of retailers taking greater control over their retail presence, property records show. The vacant, 24-acre parcel at 5253 Seminole Pratt Whitney Road sits within Minto Communities’ Westlake master development. The 188,779-square-foot Walmart development will include a grocery store, pharmacy, garden center, automotive center and vision center as well as a 1,620-square-foot gas station and a convenience store. The Westlake City Council approved the plans in April. The 3,800-acre Westlake master-planned community is approved for 6,500 homes and 2.2 million square feet of commercial development, about half of which has been sold. The population of Westlake has grown to just over 9,000 last year, up from just 912 in 2020, according to the U.S. Census. “As Westlake reaches critical mass, the market is taking notice,” John Carter, senior vice president of Minto Communities USA, said in a statement. “We want to be selective as to what types of businesses come into the city, focusing on those that add real value for our residents.” In January, Minto Communities sold a 10.6-acres site to Lowe’s for $7.5 million. The home improvement retailer will build a 107,547-square-foot store and a 26,601-square-foot outdoor garden center. The parcel, adjacent to Walmart’s new site, will also house the company’s regional headquarters. The acquisitions are part of a broader trend of retailers purchasing their store sites as higher interest rates curb competition from investors and companies look to hedge against rising rents. Since 2023, Publix has spent more than $400 million buying out its landlords. In June, the grocer paid $24 million for a 71,191-square-foot, open-air retail center in Boynton Beach, where it operates a 46,031-square-foot store. A representative for Walmart did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechik
bullets: Walmart acquires 24-acre Westlake (Palm Beach County FL) development land for $11.7M
Westlake master plan: 6,500 homes approved; population surged from 912 (2020) to 9,000+ (2024)
Retail-led (188K SF Walmart) infrastructure anchors master-planned residential growth trajectory
stories.summary: Walmart paid $11.7M for 24 acres in Westlake, a master-planned community in western Palm Beach County, to build a 188,779 SF retail center including grocery, pharmacy, and gas station. Westlake's population has exploded from 912 residents in 2020 to over 9,000 in 2024, with 6,500 homes and 2.2M SF of commercial development approved across the 3,800-acre master plan. The Walmart anchoring signals critical mass attainment and accelerating infrastructure investment.
stories.impact: Westlake's rapid population growth (nearly 10x in 4 years) and now-anchored retail infrastructure create a strong demand signal for multifamily development in western Palm Beach County. Master-planned communities with retail anchors and fast population growth typically see rent growth acceleration; developer should evaluate remaining residential parcels or joint-venture opportunities before land and construction costs rise further in response to proven demand.

stories.title: Talonvest Secures $47.6M Loan for 6-Property Texas Self-Storage Portfolio
stories.excerpt: Talonvest Capital secured a $47.6 million permanent loan on behalf of The Jenkins Organization and Clark Investment Group for a six-property self-storage portfolio located across five high-growth Texas markets, including Austin, McKinney, Frisco, Houston (shown) and Bee Cave. The institutional-quality portfolio totals more than 600,000 net rentable square feet. Talonvest identified a floating-rate financing structure from a large bank that aligned with the sponsor’s long-term ownership strategy. The financing features five consecutive one-year extension options, is non-recourse, includes interest-only payments throughout the full loan term, and has no prepayment penalties or costs. The structure gives ownership significant flexibility to respond to interest-rate and capital-market conditions as they evolve while continuing to execute its long-term business plan. Thomas Sherlock, Kim Bishop, Carson Kurland, and Lauren Maehler were among the Talonvest team members responsible for the financing. This transaction contributes to more than $256 million in financings that Talonvest has successfully closed over the past 30 days. The post Talonvest Secures $47.6M Loan for 6-Property Texas Self-Storage Portfolio appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Talonvest closes $47.6M permanent loan on 6-property TX self-storage portfolio, 600K+ SF
Portfolio spans Austin, McKinney, Frisco, Houston, Bee Cave—all high-growth Texas markets
Floating-rate structure with 1-year extensions, interest-only, non-recourse reflects lender flexibility amid rate uncertainty
stories.summary: Talonvest Capital secured a $47.6M permanent loan for a six-property self-storage portfolio totaling over 600,000 net rentable SF across Austin, McKinney, Frisco, Houston, and Bee Cave. The financing is non-recourse, features floating-rate terms with five consecutive one-year extension options, interest-only payments, and no prepayment penalties. The structure signals lender willingness to accommodate sponsors with flexibility in a moderating rate environment.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance. However, lender appetite for floating-rate structures and interest-only terms in self-storage (a lower-leverage, stable asset class) suggests capital availability and pricing flexibility for multifamily sponsors in high-growth Texas markets. Monitor comparable loan terms for multifamily development or value-add plays in same metros (Austin, Frisco, Houston) to assess refinance and permanent financing feasibility.

stories.title: KDC, Pillar Adding 225K-SF Building to Allen Office Park
stories.excerpt: KDC and Pillar Commercial have formed a partnership to develop One Bethany North, a new planned Class A office project in the Watters Creek Office Park in Allen, Texas. The Watters Creek Office Park is a 17-acre, multi-phase, Class A corporate office park with two existing buildings, and One Bethany North on the way. The nine-story office tower will include approximately 225,000 square feet of office and common area space. The development will also feature an outdoor courtyard with pickleball courts, putting greens and ample seating designed to activate the exterior elements and enhance walkability to the Watters Creek mixed-use district. A 3,500 square-foot restaurant is also planned as part of the development. One Bethany North will feature a tenant lounge, conference facilities and an upscale fitness center. The property site is directly across the street from the Delta by Marriott Convention Center Hotel. Pillar Commercial will lead the marketing and leasing effort for the new office development. The post KDC, Pillar Adding 225K-SF Building to Allen Office Park appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: KDC & Pillar develop One Bethany North: 225K SF, 9-story Class A office tower in Allen TX
Watters Creek Office Park: 17-acre multi-phase park with 3,500 SF restaurant, amenity-rich design
Site directly across from Delta by Marriott Convention Center Hotel; mixed-use activation focus
stories.summary: KDC and Pillar Commercial are partnering to develop One Bethany North, a 225,000 SF, nine-story Class A office tower in Watters Creek Office Park in Allen, Texas. The project includes a 3,500 SF ground-floor restaurant, outdoor courtyard with pickleball and putting greens, tenant lounge, conference facilities, and upscale fitness center. The tower sits across from a Delta by Marriott convention center hotel, positioning it within a mixed-use, hospitality-anchored district.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance. However, strong office development activity in Allen (a Dallas suburb) indicates sustained corporate demand and workforce inflow. Monitor Allen for multifamily absorption rates and rent trends; convention-adjacent office parks often drive hotel and hospitality worker demand, creating secondary multifamily demand in surrounding submarkets. Office anchoring can precede or support mixed-use residential development nearby.

stories.title: Scottsdale Schwab Offices Undergoing $11.7M Revamp
stories.excerpt: Charles Schwab Corp. is investing millions into an extensive renovation of a nearly 84,000-square-foot office space in north Scottsdale where the firm is planning a major Arizona expansion. The Dallas Business Journal reports the financing services company filed a permit for $11.7 million in tenant improvements at the Two Scottsdale Landing office complex at 8701 E. Hartford Drive off Pima and Bell roads. The Class B, Two Scottsdale Landing office complex is adjacent to the 124-acre Mack Innovation Park, where Toy Barn is working toward developing its largest luxury car storage facility and electric vehicle maker Rivian is opening its first Scottsdale service and repair facility. It’s also near the future site of Taser maker Axon Enterprise Inc.’s massive headquarters project. Dallas-based Schwab is one of the largest financial companies in the U.S. with more than $13 trillion in assets under management. The post Scottsdale Schwab Offices Undergoing $11.7M Revamp appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Charles Schwab invests $11.7M tenant improvements at Two Scottsdale Landing office complex
84K SF space; major Schwab Arizona expansion; $13T+ assets under management
Adjacent to Mack Innovation Park (Rivian EV service center, Toy Barn luxury storage); near Axon HQ project
stories.summary: Charles Schwab is investing $11.7M in tenant improvements at a nearly 84,000 SF office space in north Scottsdale at Two Scottsdale Landing, signaling a major Arizona expansion for the Dallas-based financial services firm. The site is adjacent to Mack Innovation Park (home to Rivian's first Scottsdale service center and Toy Barn's EV storage facility) and near the future headquarters campus of Axon Enterprise Inc. (Taser maker).
stories.impact: Schwab's large-scale office expansion and capital commitment in north Scottsdale signal sustained corporate inflow and high-wage job creation in Phoenix. Proximity to Rivian service, Axon HQ, and innovation-focused tenants suggests talent clustering and premium office/mixed-use development momentum. Multifamily developer should monitor Scottsdale north-corridor employment growth, wage levels, and residential absorption; corporate expansions of this scale typically drive 12–24 month lag in rental demand and rent growth in nearby submarkets.

stories.title: Suburban Office Leads U.S. Pricing Gains in June 2026
stories.excerpt: Led by suburban office properties, U.S. commercial property prices moved higher in June, with the RCA CPPI US National All Property Index rising 0.9% from a year earlier, MSCI Real Assets reported. The index gained 0.7% in the second quarter from Q1, implying a faster annualized growth pace of 2.6%. “Borrowing costs in the U.S. appear anchored at an elevated level, with the Federal Reserve holding its policy rate steady under new chairman Kevin Warsh,” reported MSCI Real Assets. Despite this, office prices continued rising in June, with suburban prices posting annual growth of 3.0%. While CBD office prices rose at the same monthly pace as their suburban counterparts, CBD pricing remains 50% below its March 20922 peak, a sharper drawdown than the 15% gap seen in suburban assets. Retail prices fell 0.1% from a year earlier in the sixth consecutive monthly decline, reflecting the sharper monthly drops in Q4 2025 more than current conditions. Industrial prices turned negative on an annual basis in June, falling 0.4%, down from a recent peak rate of 7.5% in June 2024. Apartment prices fell 1.7% in June from a year earlier, the 10th consecutive month of annual declines. The index dropped 1.2% from Q1, a change that annualizes to a more pronounced decline of 4.8%. The post Suburban Office Leads U.S. Pricing Gains in June 2026 appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: RCA CPPI: apartment prices fell 1.7% YoY in June 2026 (10 consecutive monthly declines)
Suburban office +3.0% YoY; CBD office +0.0% monthly but 50% below March 2022 peak
Retail -0.1% YoY; industrial -0.4% YoY; elevated Fed rate environment anchors borrowing costs
stories.summary: According to MSCI Real Assets' RCA CPPI index, U.S. apartment prices fell 1.7% year-over-year in June 2026, marking the 10th consecutive month of annual declines. Suburban office properties posted 3.0% annual growth, while CBD office prices remain 50% below their March 2022 peak despite recent modest gains. Retail prices fell 0.1% YoY, and industrial declined 0.4% YoY. Borrowing costs remain elevated as the Federal Reserve holds its policy rate steady under chairman Kevin Warsh.
stories.impact: Apartment price declines over 10 consecutive months signal persistent oversupply and/or weakening rent growth across U.S. markets. Elevated and anchored borrowing costs continue to pressure development returns and refinance values. Developer should reassess underwriting assumptions, target markets with stronger employment/inflow (Austin, DFW, Phoenix, Southeast) where supply/demand remain tighter, and consider opportunistic acquisitions of distressed or underperforming properties. Cap-rate compression may provide entry points where yield is attractive relative to risk.

stories.title: Vornado Foresees $350-per-Foot Rents at Park Avenue Office Tower: Earnings
stories.excerpt: Vornado Realty Trust announced Tuesday morning that it could levy as much as $350 per square foot at one of its latest office developments, at a time when rents over $300 a square foot at trophy properties are becoming the norm. 350 Park Avenue, which Vornado is developing with Ken Griffin’s Citadel and Rudin, may be renting for $350 per square foot, and Roth said he has confidence the building will still see leasing due to lack of supply and strong demand in the Class A office market. The news came during Vornado’s second-quarter earnings call. One investor on the call, after adding up all investments in the structure, asked for confirmation that Vornado would start the asking rent at $350, which Vornado Chairman Steven Roth confirmed as accurate. “The fact that there’s a scarcity of new supply, and the combination of the construction costs, interest rates, et cetera, require a very high rent for a new building,” Roth said. “That will cause the great, well-located, older buildings to go up and drive [leasing] enormously. And obviously, that’s the reason we bought Park Avenue Plaza.” Vornado began developing the property at the end of the fourth quarter of 2025, aiming for 1.85 million square feet of office. During the earnings call, Vornado reported that net income decreased to $16.4 million in the second quarter of 2026, compared to $743.8 million over the same period in 2025, despite strong performance elsewhere on its balance sheet. Funds from operations (FFO), however, reached $144 million in the second quarter, compared to $120.9 million year-over-year. Revenue saw an increase as well, rising to $462.2 million in the three months ending June 30, in contrast to $441.4 million in the second quarter of 2025. Vornado attributed the slide in net income to an $803.2 million master lease of 770 Broadway to New York University, but executives and investors on the call did not seem fazed by that individual metric. bullets: Vornado forecasts $350/SF rents at 350 Park Avenue (Manhattan office tower with Citadel, Rudin)
CEO Steven Roth cites scarcity of new supply and strong Class A demand justifying premium pricing
Construction costs and interest rates require high rents; older Class A buildings benefit from supply scarcity
stories.summary: Vornado Realty Trust announced that its 350 Park Avenue office development (built in partnership with Citadel and Rudin) could command rents as high as $350 per square foot. CEO Steven Roth emphasized that the scarcity of new office supply, combined with strong demand in the Class A market and elevated construction and financing costs, justifies premium pricing. Roth further noted that the supply constraint will bolster rents at well-located, high-quality older buildings in Manhattan.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance, but signals important capital and cost dynamics: sustained elevated construction costs and interest rates are making new trophy office development financially marginal unless rents reach unprecedented levels ($300+/SF). This constraint on office supply (and its high cost) may redirect institutional capital and developer focus to multifamily, where higher yields and lower entry costs offer better risk-adjusted returns. Monitor Manhattan office development feasibility closely; if office rents remain below required levels, capital will flow to residential in high-demand metros.

stories.title: The Decisions That Changed Everything
stories.excerpt: People often ask me what the secret was to building a business that sold more than three times the number of investment properties than any other firm in New York City for 14 consecutive years. They expect the answer to involve a particular strategy, a recruiting philosophy or some proprietary marketing technique. The truth is much simpler. When I look back over more than four decades in commercial real estate, I don’t believe my career was built by thousands of decisions. It was built by a handful. Most days were ordinary. I showed up, worked hard, made calls, met clients, negotiated transactions and tried to improve a little each day. But, every so often, a decision came along that permanently altered the direction of everything that followed. Those are the moments that shape careers, companies and, ultimately, lives. The first came before my career even began. As a student at Wharton, I thought I wanted to become an investment banker. That was the prestigious path. Then I spent a summer at Coldwell Banker in commercial real estate. I loved the entrepreneurial nature of the business, the direct connection between effort and results, and the opportunity to build relationships rather than simply analyze transactions. I returned the next two summers and joined Coldwell Banker full time after graduation in 1984. Looking back, that single decision determined the course of the next 42 years (and counting). A few years later, Paul Massey and I decided we wanted to start our own company. We walked into Chemical Bank seeking a loan to finance our dream. They laughed at us. No one wanted to lend money to two young brokers with little more than ambition. Instead of abandoning the idea, we spent the next two years saving every dollar we could. By November 1988, we had accumulated $400,000 and launched Massey Knakal. At the time, it felt like an enormous leap into the unknown. bullets: Paul Massey (Massey Knakal) reflects on 40+ year CRE career: strategy built on handful of pivotal decisions
Early choice to pursue commercial real estate over investment banking shaped career trajectory
Essay on decision-making, entrepreneurship, and long-term business building; limited transaction details
stories.summary: Paul Massey, former principal at Massey Knakal (which sold more investment properties than any other firm in NYC for 14 consecutive years), reflects on a 40+ year career in commercial real estate. He argues that his success stemmed not from thousands of routine decisions but from a handful of pivotal moments, starting with choosing commercial real estate over investment banking as a student at Wharton. The article emphasizes the power of strategic decision-making and entrepreneurial mindset in long-term business building.
stories.impact: Primarily editorial/thought leadership; no immediate market signal. Relevance to multifamily developer is strategic mindset only: decisions around market selection, capital deployment timing, and partnership structuring are rare, high-impact moments that define firm trajectory. Read as a reminder to focus on market fundamentals and long-term value creation rather than transaction volume.

stories.title: Urban Standard Capital Grows $200M Credit Facility With Western Alliance Bank
stories.excerpt: Urban Standard Capital has deepened its relationship with a major Arizona bank. Commercial Observer can first report that Urban Standard Capital has increased its aggregate financing capacity for transitional commercial real estate loans with Western Alliance Bank — a Phoenix-based regional bank with $90 billion of assets — to $200 million through three separate funds. The two lenders began their business relationship in 2020. Seth Weissman, founder and managing partner at Urban Standard Capital, a New York-based CRE private credit firm, told CO that the coordinated lending capacity has steadily increased from $40 million to $125 million over the last six years. He added that he expects the credit facility to continue to aid his firm in making loan originations to sponsors for tailored financing projects, which have typically fallen into the $15 million to $20 million range. “It’s a capital partnership that allows us to lower our cost of capital and be able to be more flexible and service our clients better,” said Weissman. “It helps me to deliver speed and flexibility to our borrowers and increases our capacity for lending.” Weissman could not estimate a number of loans the credit facility will ultimately provide, as he noted that the facility recycles each time previous loans pay off. “If I invest $200 million, and a loan pays off for $20 million, I can draw that money again, and I’ll probably turn this money over four times, so it’s probably $800 million of lending power over the life of the arrangement,” said Weissmann. Since beginning its business in 2014, Urban Standard Capital has originated $2.3 billion in loans for more than 260 real estate projects. “That progression didn’t happen overnight,” said Weissman. “It was earned through consistent performance, disciplined underwriting, and delivering on what we said we would do.” Ian Hawk, New York market manager for Western Alliance Bank, noted in a statement that his firm has “built a strong relationship”
bullets: Urban Standard Capital increases financing capacity with Western Alliance Bank to $200M (from $125M)
Three-fund structure; capacity grew from $40M over 6 years; regional bank-CRE lender partnership deepens
Typical loan size: $15M–$20M for transitional CRE; lender seeks cost reduction, flexibility for sponsors
stories.summary: Urban Standard Capital has increased its aggregate transitional CRE financing capacity with Phoenix-based Western Alliance Bank (assets: $90B) to $200M through three separate funds. The coordinated capacity has grown from $40M six years ago to $125M and now $200M. Founder Seth Weissman notes the facility lowers his firm's cost of capital and enables faster, more flexible loan originations in the $15M–$20M range.
stories.impact: Regional bank appetite for transitional CRE lending (and willingness to grow committed capital) signals capital availability for development and value-add multifamily sponsors in Western markets (Arizona and nearby). Monitor Western Alliance and similar regional bank product offerings; growing permanent and construction financing capacity in the $15M–$20M range supports mid-sized multifamily development. However, no evidence of rate/term changes; verify that pricing and spreads remain competitive relative to national lenders.

stories.title: Hines Reveals Plans for SouthPark Mixed-Use Venture
stories.excerpt: Hines has plans for a mixed-use development called The Gallery, which will include a 250,000-square-foot office tower; a 19-story, 302-unit multifamily tower; and 50,000 square feet of retail use. The project in SouthPark will replace a single-story retail building at 6601 and 6555 Carnegie Blvd., which currently houses three food-and-beverage purveyors. The Charlotte Business Journal reports the ground-floor retail will surround a plaza that opens up to the street and the multifamily tower will be within walking distance to neighborhood amenities like Symphony Park and The Specialty Shops. Office tower amenities will include private terraces, a shared sky terrace and lounge, conference and training facilities, fitness offerings and direct access to ground-floor retail. JLL’s John Ball, Karah Tanneberger and Claiborne Mulhern will lead office leasing efforts. Hines will handle retail leasing. Hines is developing the site in partnership with Harris Land Co., which owns the property. Hines does not yet have a timeline for construction. The post Hines Reveals Plans for SouthPark Mixed-Use Venture appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Hines develops The Gallery SouthPark Charlotte: 250K SF office, 302-unit multifamily, 50K SF retail
19-story multifamily tower; ground-floor retail plaza opens to street; mixed-use activation
Partnership with Harris Land Co.; location near Symphony Park and The Specialty Shops; no construction timeline
stories.summary: Hines is developing The Gallery, a mixed-use project in Charlotte's SouthPark neighborhood comprising a 250,000 SF office tower, a 19-story multifamily tower with 302 units, and 50,000 SF of retail. The project replaces a single-story retail building and features ground-floor retail surrounding a street-facing plaza. The multifamily tower will be within walking distance to neighborhood amenities including Symphony Park and The Specialty Shops. Hines is partnering with Harris Land Co.; no construction timeline has been announced.
stories.impact: Mixed-use development in SouthPark (Charlotte's established affluent office/retail submarket) signals continued urban mixed-use preference among major developers. The 302-unit multifamily component in a retail-anchored, office-proximate setting targets white-collar renter demographic. Developer should monitor Charlotte multifamily absorption and rent trends in SouthPark; if The Gallery leases office and retail at strong pace, multifamily absorption will accelerate, compressing supply and supporting rent growth. SouthPark remains a strong market for Class A multifamily development.
